Tides and tempers on the estuary

Nobody on the estuary trusts the weather forecast, but everybody trusts the tide table pinned beside the chandler's door. It tells the fishermen when to leave, the ferrymen when to wait and the children when the causeway will be dry enough to cross.

Arguments are settled by it as well. A dispute over a mooring was ended last autumn when a retired teacher produced the almanac and pointed to the exact minute the water had turned.

The tide table is printed by a family firm that has used the same press for ninety years. Its owner insists that accuracy is a matter of manners.

Every January the printers walk the shoreline with a notebook, checking the new figures against the marks on the old stone steps. Sometimes the sea disagrees with the mathematics, and then the steps are right.

Visitors find the habit quaint. Locals consider it ordinary good sense, and a little overdue in most other parts of life.

By the time the evening ferry docks, the lamps along the quay are lit and the table beside the door has already been updated for tomorrow.
